overview: The Naples entry samples the southern mainland kingdom during Spanish viceregal rule. It is more than the city of Naples, and it should not be silently merged with Sicily. Spanish government lasted from 1503 to 1707, beyond the map’s 1530 to 1700 interval. Palace archaeology, banking records and music schools offer unusually concrete windows into life in its capital.

periods.title: A kingdom governed by viceroys
periods.summary: The Spanish monarchy governed Naples through viceroys. The imported map begins decades after Spanish rule started in 1503.

periods.title: A viceregal capital
periods.summary: A new royal palace began in 1600. Seventeenth-century Naples supported financial, charitable and musical institutions alongside court government; the map interval ends before Spanish rule did.

sections.title: A palace well and a busy city

items.text: The Royal Palace begun in 1600 was designed by Domenico Fontana as a residence for the Spanish viceroys. A royal building did not mean the Spanish king personally lived there year-round: the viceroy governed on his behalf.

Excavations in 1999 to 2000 recovered around 5,000 objects and ceramic fragments from a well at the older palace. The well probably first supplied water and later received rubbish. Broken things can be wonderfully informative: an archaeologist’s useful evidence may once have been somebody else’s unwanted mess.

The palace-well finds include pottery from Naples and other Italian production centers, as well as Spanish wares from places such as Manises and Valencia. They reveal connections through objects used or discarded at this particular site. A palace deposit is not a random sample of every Neapolitan kitchen.

A blue-and-white Chinese porcelain bowl from the late sixteenth century appeared among the well’s finds. It shows that an object could reach Naples through long-distance exchange. One bowl does not establish who transported it, who ate from it or whether a Chinese community lived beside the palace.

Naples’ water administration left records of expenditure on the Carmignano aqueduct in 1629 and later water concessions. These documents show that moving and allocating water required money and rules. They cannot, by themselves, tell us what kind of toilet or wash space an individual family possessed.

The Monte della Pietà began in 1539 to make interest-free loans against pledged possessions for people in need. It later accepted deposits and received royal recognition as a bank in 1584. Charity and finance developed together rather than occupying entirely separate worlds.

Household belongings could become temporary security for a loan. The Pietà accepted linen, wool and silk as well as precious objects. The bank archive distinguishes limited interest-free lending from other loans that charged interest: “charitable bank” did not mean that every transaction was free.

The Annunziata bank, established in 1587, helped support an orphanage, hospital and girls’ school. Another bank founded in 1589 was connected with the Incurabili hospital. Financial records therefore preserve practical links between savings, credit and the care of vulnerable people.

The early Neapolitan conservatories cared for poor or abandoned children. Music formed part of their religious activities in the sixteenth century. The name later became strongly associated with professional musical training, but these institutions began with a wider charitable purpose.

During the seventeenth century, conservatory musicians increasingly performed for paying patrons, and musical training attracted outside pupils. Performance could support an institution as well as teach a trade. This does not mean all Neapolitan children learned music or that every child in care became a celebrated composer.

sections.title: A written voice and its stories

items.text: Giambattista Basile’s Lo cunto de li cunti appeared after his death in installments from 1634 to 1636. Written in Neapolitan, its fifty tales reshaped storytelling traditions into elaborate literature. Stories can preserve language and imaginative worlds without being literal reports of daily events.

The title “Lo Cunto de li Cunti” means “The Tale of Tales.” This short Neapolitan sample uses Latin letters and is attested in the original title transcribed in a later scholarly edition. Its repeated word cunto makes the title sound like an invitation to settle in for another story.

Basile’s collection also includes verse interludes voiced by figures such as cooks, servants and household officials. Their presence brings work and social hierarchy into the literary performance. These are crafted voices, however, not interviews with real palace employees or a census of ordinary family life.

ending.text: Spanish viceregal rule ended in 1707, rather than at the atlas’s 1700 cutoff. The Kingdom of Naples and its population continued under subsequent rulers. This entry’s ending therefore describes a change of government, not the destruction of Naples or the disappearance of its culture.
